meta.regime: Yesterday this file said the synchronised hawkish repricing was complete and that completion, not direction, should size positions. Today supplies the proof and a fresh binary: Japan delivered the one print that could still change a policy leg - September core CPI at 2.1%, above the 2% target for the first time since December, with the ex-food-and-energy measure jumping to 2.4% from 1.9% - and USD/JPY went UP 0.16% to 157.015. Every move on the board was under 0.30%. Underneath that calm, two things did move: US ten-year yields broke below 5% to 4.9700 while the Nasdaq fell 2.60% to 26,009 and the VIX rose 14.09% to 19.03, and neither gold nor the yen caught a bid on the way down - gold is 4,007.55 and has erased its 2026 gain. That is de-risking, not haven demand, and it is the single most useful tell on this board. The live catalyst is Moody's, which reviews France's Aa3 negative rating today with most economists expecting a cut to A1, into an OAT at 5.0760 and a spread to Bunds of 173.95 basis points.
meta.nextBigEvent: Moody's France rating review today is the only unpriced binary before the weekend. France has carried Aa3 with a negative outlook since October 2025, the scheduled review date is today, and economists quoted by Boursorama call a hold unlikely with a cut to A1 very plausible; the agency does not publish a time in advance, so it typically lands after the European close. It matters because the market has spent three sessions refusing to sell the euro on French credit - EUR/USD is 1.12082 and down only 0.07% while the OAT-Bund spread widened another 15 basis points to 173.95 - and has instead sold the equity, with EU50 down 1.96% today and 2.87% on the week against a DAX up 0.13% on the week. A downgrade tests whether that separation holds. After that the board empties until Wednesday October 28, when Australian Q3 CPI at 00:30 UTC, the RBNZ Monetary Policy Review at 01:00 UTC, the Bank of Canada with a full Monetary Policy Report at 13:45 UTC and the FOMC at 18:00 UTC all land inside eighteen hours, then the ECB on October 29 at 13:15 UTC and the Bank of Japan on October 30 at 03:00 UTC with a fresh Quarterly Outlook Report.

dailyRead: The most important thing that happened today is that the best piece of news a currency has received all week produced nothing. Japan's September national CPI, flagged in this file yesterday as the gate, cleared it: core inflation printed 2.1% against 1.7% in August, matching consensus and taking the measure above the Bank of Japan's 2% target for the first time since December, headline rose to 2.1% from 1.9%, and the narrow measure excluding fresh food and energy jumped to 2.4% from 1.9%. TradingEconomics also now carries Japanese inflation expectations at 3.5% against 2.7%. That last number is the one that matters, because Deputy Governor Himino said two days ago that underlying inflation was almost at 2%, and 2.4% says it is there. And USD/JPY rose 0.16% to 157.015. The yen was mid-pack, gaining only against the Aussie. Yesterday the yen led all seven of its crosses in anticipation of exactly this print; today it was delivered and the market took profit. This is why JPY goes to plus 1 rather than plus 2, and why every yen leg in this file is capped at LOW-MED: the fundamental case is now confirmed rather than expected, swaps had December 18 at roughly 75-80% before the data and analysts uniformly expect a hold on October 30, so the hike is a December story that a 157 handle has largely absorbed. USD/JPY has held a 157-159 range for the whole of October and has not traded above 159.00 since Finance Minister Katayama's October 15 warning, with 160 treated as the intervention trigger. Selling the bottom of that range on confirmed news is the wrong side of the distribution; the yen is worth owning against the euro and the franc, where the other leg has its own problem, rather than against a dollar whose own range floor is holding. The second story is the one the market is actually trading, and it is not in FX at all. US ten-year yields broke below 5% to 4.9700, down about 17 basis points on Thursday and roughly 12 from the 5.0910 this file carried two sessions ago, and that happened alongside a Nasdaq down 2.60% to 26,009 - now 5.8% below its October 6 record - an S&P 500 down 1.21% to 7,663 and a VIX up 14.09% to 19.03. In a classic risk-off session falling yields and falling equities buy gold and buy the yen. Neither happened. Gold fell to 4,007.55, down 0.43% on the session, 3.81% on the week and 6.25% on the month, and is now down 2.54% on the year, which means the metal has given back its entire 2026 gain; silver fell 1.51% to 53.762 and is down 15.76% on the month, widening the gold-silver ratio to about 74.5 from 72.6. A tape where equities, gold and silver all fall together while the dollar index adds 0.06% to 101.710 is a positioning unwind, not a flight to safety, and that reading is what keeps both metals SHORT and keeps conviction on every haven-shaped trade in this file deliberately low. Gold sitting a few dollars above 4,000 is the level to watch; a clean break would be the first genuine trend signal the metals complex has given since the war began. Third, the euro. The credit story got worse again and the currency again declined to care. The French ten-year is 5.0760 against a Bund that fell to 3.3365, which takes the spread to 173.95 basis points - another 15 basis points wider than yesterday and the widest this file has recorded - and France now borrows 47.4 basis points more dearly than Italy, whose BTP is 4.6020. The OAT closed above 5% on both Wednesday and Thursday, the highest closing level since July 2002. And EUR/USD fell only 0.07% to 1.12082. What is new and genuinely tradeable is that Moody's reviews France today: the rating is Aa3 with a negative outlook dating from October 2025, this is the scheduled review date, and the economists quoted by Boursorama call a hold unlikely and a cut to A1 very plausible. So the euro keeps minus 1 - the Governing Council has said a 2.50% deposit rate already sits inside its neutral estimates, September HICP of 3.8% has no wage mechanism behind it with negotiated wage growth at 2.44% from 2.56%, and EU gas is 91.20 euros per megawatt hour and up 21.70% on the month - but the expression stays where the market has chosen to pay, which is the index. EU50 fell 1.96% to 6,092.70 and is down 2.87% on the week; the DAX fell 1.07% to 25,300.10 but is up 0.13% on the week. Three points of weekly divergence between two European equity indices is the French leg dominating outright, and that is the cleanest paid expression of this story on the board. Fourth, Canada keeps plus 2 and the top of the board, but with one honest revision. Brent rose another 0.59% to 113.840 and is up 3.62% on the week and 6.79% on the month, which is the Macklem argument from October 17 - that the Bank expects to raise its quarterly inflation forecast significantly on persistently high crude - getting stronger every day against the 75 dollars the Bank assumed in July. WTI is back above 100 at 100.208. What has changed is the pricing: yesterday this file reported Bloomberg swap data as high as 87% for an October 28 hike, and today's sources are less uniform - Hashtag Investing has swaps near 80% as of October 21, StoneX is explicitly more cautious on the grounds that softer Canadian core gives the Bank room to hold, and RateProbability's own table showed 40.8% for the meeting against an 81% headline, a discrepancy this report cannot reconcile. That dispersion cuts in the loonie's favour rather than against it. A meeting at 98%, like the RBNZ's, has nothing left to pay; a meeting somewhere between 40% and 87% still does, and Canada is the only one of the four hawkish banks where that is true alongside a two-point score gap to the euro. The counter-evidence is unchanged and real - September employment minus 68.3k after minus 41.7k, unemployment 6.5%, core CPI down to 2.2% with Median 2.0% and Trimmed 1.9%, a ten-year at 3.7870 and RBC still forecasting no move until 2027 - so this is a position to hold against the euro and the franc, not a reason to chase USD/CAD at 1.40136. Fifth, the two antipodeans split for the second day. New Zealand was the strongest currency in the session, up 0.29% against the yen, 0.27% against the franc, 0.15% against the loonie and 0.14% against the dollar at 0.56897, finally rallying into a meeting it had refused to rally into all week; pricing for the October 28 hike to 3.00% runs anywhere from 80% on Admiral's October 20 read to 85% on BBH's October 22 swaps read to 98% at StoneX, and BBH notes more than 100 basis points of tightening priced over twelve months. NZD holds plus 1 and no more, because at that pricing the hike itself pays nothing and only an explicitly marked-up Q4 track would. Australia was the weakest currency for the second consecutive session - AUD/USD minus 0.20% to 0.70062, AUD/NZD minus 0.29%, AUD/CAD minus 0.18% - and this is where the file deliberately does not cut again. Yesterday AUD came down from plus 2 to plus 1 on exactly one session of underperformance. A second session is not new information, and the forecast community has moved the other way in the meantime: Goldman Sachs has switched from no change to a 25 basis point hike to 4.85% on November 3, ANZ and Westpac expect a hike, CBA expects a hold and NAB has a hold with a hike as the risk. Market pricing is correspondingly scattered, 51% on Bloomberg data cited by the ABC, 56% at Pound Sterling Live, 23.2% on an ActionForex OIS snapshot from Tuesday evening. That spread is the point: the Aussie's meeting is the only genuinely two-sided one left, and the whole thesis resolves on Q3 CPI at 00:30 UTC on Wednesday, where the RBA's August forecast was about 0.8% for the quarterly trimmed mean, the market is at 0.9-1.0%, and Hauser has already said it will run hotter than expected. Copper, the terms-of-trade leg, bounced 0.62% to 6.4017 but is still down 1.98% on the week and 4.79% on the month. AUD/NZD at 1.23131 is the single highest-information pair on the board next Wednesday, because the two decisions are twelve hours apart and the pricing gap between them is enormous. Sterling holds plus 1 unchanged: November 5 is locked at 93-98%, the UK ten-year at 5.3396 is still the highest yield in this file, December has faded to roughly 45-48% from 58%, and September retail sales were released at 06:00 UTC against a minus 0.1% consensus from 0.5% but the actual had not reached TradingEconomics or search at the time of writing, so it is not verifiable here. The dollar and the franc both stay at zero. December Fed pricing is about 90% on CME FedWatch - 75.2% for 25 basis points plus 15.2% for 50, against 9.6% unchanged - October 28 is a hold at 84-93.5%, the Committee is in blackout, and Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan both carry a December quarter point. On the franc, yesterday's open item is now closed: this file could not retrieve the SNB Summary of Monetary Policy Discussions and said so, and Bloomberg has since reported its content - the Bank judged that an increased willingness to intervene was no longer necessary because war-induced haven flows into the franc had ebbed, and it flagged the franc's appeal as a carry-trade funding currency. That confirms the September language change rather than extending it, most analysts see no SNB hike before 2028, and EUR/CHF at 0.92095 is back near the zone where the Bank previously threatened to step up intervention - which is the standing risk to every short-EUR/CHF ticket here. Commodities close the picture and they are the one place the war premium is still being paid. Hormuz is on day 236. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed seven tankers damaged in a single day, which Iranian state media called a record; UKMTO confirmed two, the claim is otherwise unverified, and President Trump publicly accused Iran of inventing strikes to drive up oil prices. USNI News, citing IMO figures, reports 27 attacks on commercial shipping in October, the highest monthly total since the war began in late February. IMF PortWatch logged four transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85. Iran's seven conditions for reopening the strait have been on the table since early October and Washington has not publicly accepted them. The cleanest tickets today are short EUR/CAD on the widest score gap on the board, short EUR/JPY and short EUR/CHF where a confirmed policy leg or a haven bid faces a rating review tonight, short EU50 as the paid expression of the French curve, and long USOIL. The ones to size down are every yen leg against the dollar, where the news is now in the price and the range floor is holding, and anything that needs the Aussie to rally before Wednesday morning.

The only upside is a statement that explicitly marks up the Q4 track, where economists see the annual rate back above 4% against the Bank's own 3.9%; the downside is any trimming of that probability, which would be one-way. Express it against the euro, which has a rating review tonight, and against the loonie, where the other leg has a decision on the same day that is much less paid for.

USD.note: TE re-verified the fed funds target range at 3.75-4.00%, upper bound 4.00%, after the unanimous September 16 hike - the first since 2023 - with a majority of the September projections showing one more increase before year-end. The Committee is in blackout into the October 27-28 meeting and has no mechanism to reprice on its own words. What moved today was the curve, not the pricing: the ten-year broke below 5% to 4.9700, down about 17 basis points on Thursday, while the Nasdaq fell 2.60% and the VIX rose 14.09% to 19.03. Falling nominal yields with a December hike still 90% priced is the market taking growth risk out rather than policy risk out, and it is consistent with gold falling at the same time. EUR.when: October 29 at 13:15 UTC with the press conference at 13:45 UTC, where the ECB Watch tool shows a 93% probability of the deposit rate staying at 2.50%. December 17 is the projection meeting and the earliest realistic move; FXStreet now carries a final 25 basis point hike there.
EUR.note: TE re-verified the ECB deposit facility rate at 2.50% after the September 10 hike, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%. The accounts of that meeting were dovish: the Council saw inflation risks skewed to the upside but stressed not signalling further moves, and noted that 2.50% already sits within staff estimates of neutral. The wage data agrees - TE has whole-economy wage growth at 3.0% from 3.4% and negotiated wage growth at 2.44% from 2.56% - so September HICP of 3.8% with 2.5% core has no second-round mechanism behind it, and FXStreet's preview argues that energy spillovers into underlying inflation remain very muted. This is still the only currency in the file whose central bank has not been repriced hawkish by the oil shock, while the euro area absorbs EU gas at 91.20 euros per megawatt hour, up 21.70% on the month, and German gas at 91.29 and up 24.69%. The sovereign problem sharpened again today without the currency responding: the OAT is 5.0760, the spread to Bunds is 173.95 basis points and Moody's reviews the Aa3 negative rating today. The October 29 press conference is where the fragmentation question gets asked at that spread, and if a downgrade lands first it is the one scheduled event that could turn the French credit story into a currency story.

GBP.note: TE re-verified Bank Rate at 3.75%. September CPI at 3.5% against a 3.4% consensus and 3.1% in August settled November, with core matching at 2.8% from 2.6% and services inflation accelerating to 3.7% from 3.4%. The composition is why this is a cap rather than a launchpad: motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier and transport did the work, which is the oil premium arriving in the UK index rather than fresh domestic pressure, and it puts 3.5% on the Bank's own roughly 3.75% fourth-quarter track rather than above it. The market responded by marking down what comes after, cutting December to roughly 45-48%, and that remains the only hawkish repricing in this file to have run in reverse. catalysts.event: United Kingdom: September CPI y/y (ONS red folder)
catalysts.note: Released above forecast at 3.5% year on year against a 3.4% consensus and 3.1% in August, carried on TradingEconomics. Core matched consensus exactly at 2.8% from 2.6% and services inflation accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4%. Transport did the work, with motor fuel prices 29.8% higher than a year earlier - the oil premium arriving in the UK index rather than fresh domestic pressure, which puts 3.5% on the Bank's own roughly 3.75% fourth-quarter track rather than above it. November 5 is settled at 93-98%, but the market used the beat to cut December to roughly 45-48% from 58%, and that remains the only hawkish repricing in this file to have run in reverse.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 CPI q/q (Stats NZ red folder)

It was the most dovish outcome available: a Bloomberg survey of 16 economists had a 3.8% median, two tenths under the RBNZ's own 3.9% projection, with cheaper petrol and diesel taking roughly 0.4 percentage points off the quarterly pace. The market raised its hike odds on it anyway, because 3.7% is still outside the 1-3% band and the hawkish case was always the Q4 fuel pass-through. Pricing for October 28 now runs 80% on Admiral's October 20 read, 85% on BBH's October 22 swaps read and 98% at StoneX.

catalysts.event: Japan: National Core CPI y/y (Statistics Bureau)
catalysts.note: The most important release of the week despite its low ForexFactory billing, and the reason the yen is upgraded today. Core inflation printed 2.1% against 1.7% in August, matching consensus and clearing the Bank of Japan's 2% target for the first time since December; headline rose to 2.1% from 1.9%; and the narrow measure excluding fresh food and energy jumped to 2.4% from 1.9% - all verified on TradingEconomics, which also now carries inflation expectations at 3.5% from 2.7%. Deputy Governor Himino said on October 21 that underlying inflation was almost at 2%, and the ex-food-and-energy figure says it has arrived. Reporting attributes the broadening to Middle East fuel costs, a weak yen and AI-related demand, with electricity subsidies still suppressing the core figure. The market reaction was the surprise: USD/JPY rose 0.16% to 157.015, because swaps already had December 18 at 75-80% and no analyst expects a move on October 30.

catalysts.event: France: Moody's scheduled review of the Aa3 sovereign rating
catalysts.note: The only unpriced binary left before the weekend and the single most tradeable event in this report. France has carried Aa3 with a negative outlook since October 2025, today is the scheduled review date published by the Agence France Tresor, and Moody's does not announce a time in advance - these decisions typically land after the European close. Economists quoted by Boursorama call a hold unlikely, with a cut to A1 described as very plausible; keeping the rating or improving the outlook are the other listed options. The context is an OAT at 5.0760 that closed above 5% on both Wednesday and Thursday for the first time since July 2002, a spread to Bunds of 173.95 basis points, and France now borrowing 47.4 basis points more dearly than Italy. The test is whether a downgrade finally makes the currency carry a story that EU50, down 2.87% on the week against a DAX up 0.13%, has been carrying alone.

Morgan both carry a December move. The Committee is in blackout until it meets. Goldman Sachs switched from no change to a 25 basis point hike to 4.85%, ANZ and Westpac expect a hike, CBA expects a hold and reads Hauser's remarks as only a temporary lift for the currency, and NAB has a hold with a hike as the risk rather than the base case. The Q3 CPI print six days earlier decides it.

Neither is a rate event, but both sit between this report and the December 9 decision that is currently 90% priced.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz is on day 236 of closure and today produced the largest single claim of the war alongside the clearest sign yet that the market has stopped treating escalation as a haven event. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed seven oil tankers were damaged in a single day, described by Iranian state media as a record: four said to have been struck and set on fire for conducting ship-to-ship transfers, three damaged in collisions with mines it says it laid. UKMTO confirmed two vessels. The remainder is unverified, no vessel names, flag states or operators were supplied, and President Trump publicly accused Iran of inventing strikes to drive up oil prices - an accusation that is itself tradeable, because it signals Washington is not treating the claim as grounds for escalation. The harder number comes from USNI News citing IMO figures: 27 attacks on commercial shipping in October, the highest monthly total since the war began in late February. IMF PortWatch logged four transits on October 18 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85. The price transmission is intact and still widening. Brent rose 0.59% to 113.840 and is up 3.62% on the week and 6.79% on the month; WTI rose 0.74% to 100.208, back above the hundred handle, leaving a 13.63 dollar spread that is the pure transit premium. European gas is where the second-round pressure lives: EU gas is 91.20 euros per megawatt hour and up 21.70% on the month, German gas 91.29 and up 24.69%, UK gas up 17.12%. That is the mechanism running from the strait into the euro area's inflation problem without touching its growth story, and it is why the ECB is the only central bank in this file the oil shock has not repriced hawkish while the euro sits at the bottom of the board. The FX read has two layers now. The first is unchanged and mechanical: energy importers with meetings inside six weeks have all been repriced hawkish, which is the Canadian, British, New Zealand and Australian stories, and the energy exporter among them - Canada - gets the terms-of-trade benefit on top, which is why CAD holds the top of the board with Brent making Macklem's October 17 argument stronger every session. The second layer is new and it is the reason conviction is capped everywhere. On a day with a record attack claim, Brent through 113, a Nasdaq down 2.60%, a VIX up 14.09% and a ten-year breaking below 5%, gold fell to 4,007.55 and silver fell 1.51% to 53.762. Gold has now erased its entire 2026 gain. A market that will not buy the inflation hedge on an escalation headline, and will not buy the yen on one either, has concluded that the war is an inflation problem the central banks will answer rather than a risk event to hide from - and is now selling the hedge because it believes the answer is coming. That belief is what every long-USOIL, short-metals and long-CAD position in this file is really expressing, and it unwinds on one headline. Iran's seven conditions for reopening the strait have been on the table since early October and Washington has not publicly accepted them; the enriched-uranium question remains the sticking point, and Britain's Ed Miliband is reported heading to talks in Turkey covering the Hormuz crisis. Acceptance would take Brent down, take the inflation forecast out of four central banks at once, and reverse the cleanest trades on this board in a single session.
